frontmatter.title: Notebook Manipulation

blocks.content: Aspose.Note enables programmatic manipulation of OneNote notebooks using Python. This page covers core operations for loading, saving, and modifying notebook structures in `.one` files via the `aspose_note_foss` package.

Developers use these capabilities to automate note organization, batch-export notes to PDF, or integrate note-taking workflows into larger Python applications. The API supports standard notebook operations such as opening existing files, adding or removing pages, and persisting changes — all from Python code.

Aspose.Note enables programmatic manipulation of notebook data using core operations: reading, writing, and modifying elements. Developers work with notebook structures and their contained pages, sections, and content elements through the `Notebook` and `Document` classes.
Load a notebook file and access its pages or child notebooks using the `Notebook` class. Iterate over the `pages` collection to inspect individual pages or nested structures.

import aspose_note_foss

notebook = aspose_note_foss.Notebook("input.one")
for page in notebook.pages:
    print(page.title)
Create a new notebook or save an existing one using the `save()` method. The `Document` class supports saving individual pages or full notebooks to disk in .one format.
Modify notebook content by updating page properties or replacing section contents. Changes are persisted when calling `save()` on the parent `Notebook` or `Document` instance.

Aspose.Note enables programmatic manipulation of OneNote notebooks using Python. Developers can load, inspect, and save notebook files with minimal code, supporting common workflows such as converting notes to PDF or iterating over notebook pages.

import aspose_note_foss

notebook = aspose_note_foss.Notebook("input.one")
print(f"Loaded notebook with {len(notebook.pages)} pages")

When working with Aspose.Note in Python, efficient memory usage and correct resource handling are essential for stable notebook manipulation. The `Notebook` class loads entire document hierarchies into memory, so large files may impact performance if not managed carefully.

items: Use `Notebook.load()` only when full document access is required; prefer `Document` for single-page operations to reduce memory footprint.
Close `Notebook` and `Document` instances explicitly using `dispose()` after processing to release unmanaged resources.
Avoid holding multiple open instances simultaneously—especially in loops—to prevent memory exhaustion.
For batch operations, process notebooks in chunks and save intermediate results to disk rather than keeping everything in memory.
